newsitem.title: USA: NZ's Birch moves to reassure U.S. investors, funds. [CORRECTED 22:52 GMT]
newsitem.headline: NZ's Birch moves to reassure U.S. investors, funds. [CORRECTED 22:52 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects headline to read Birch not Brash.)

On a global mission to reassure investors and financial institutions, New Zealand Finance Minister Bill Birch has praised the reorganisation of the finance portfolio and asserted the coalition government's commitment to "fiscal and economic responsibility".

After meeting with Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and visiting credit rating agencies Moody's and Standard and Poors, he also told a luncheon audience here that the coalition continued to welcome foreign investment and had taken strides to contain spending.
"Everyone expected more government spending and there is. But we have a clear and finite limit on government spending a clear commitment to keep to that limit," he said on Thursday.
Following years of fullsome praise for New Zealand economic reform and central bank innovations, Wall Street has greeted the new government with caution and a degree of skeptism.
"I still don't think anyone knows yet how he (Winston Peters) is going to impact," said one leading international analyst who asked not to be named.
"NZ was the shining example for a long while, but discouraging investment, changing the Reserve Bank Act and boosting spending might help end the party."
Mr Birch emphasised that little had changed since the election.
"The fiscal and economic framework has been embraced by the co-alition," he told the luncheon.
"The harshest critics of the framework had been ... the left-leaning parties and they both lost ground at the election and that was an endorsement from the public."
Mr Birch called the broadening of the Reserve Bank inflation band to 0 to 3 pct from from 0 to 2 pct a "technical adjustment to the policy target agreement and does not change the Reserve Bank Act."
The minister said he recognised there had been market aprehension about splitting the finance portfolio by creating the Treasurer post however "it is working extremely well".
"I expect the split will be an enduring feature of future governments," he said.

While Mr Peters' pre-election comments on foreign investment were poorly received internationally, Mr Birch said the "reality is that as a small trading nation we must be open and outward looking if we are going to be successful."
"Our rules for foreign investment are among the most lberal in the world," he said, before detailing the coalition's intention to retain local ownership of key state assets.
Mr Birch planned to fly to Frankfurt this week for further meetings before moving on to London.
